review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Wheat relatives harbour abundant variations that can be used for genetic improvement against diseases through complex domestication processes. Here, we report the isolation of the powdery mildew resistance gene Pm37 in common wheat through a strategy integrating map-based cloning, PacBio SMRT long-read genome sequencing, mutagenesis, barley stripe mosaic virus-induced gene silencing and stable transformation. Pm37 encodes a coiled-coil nucleotide-binding site leucine-rich repeat (CC-NBS-LRR) receptor. The cell death-inducing activity of PM37 in Nicotiana benthamiana is mainly mediated by its CC domain. De novo genome sequencing and haplotype analysis reveal that Pm37 may be derived from Triticum monococcum, and transferred into common wheat through T. timopheevii. Interestingly, Pm37 is a susceptible allele of the stem rust resistance locus Sr22, and also confers moderate resistance to leaf rust. Our findings identify a gene characterized by allelic variation-driven functional divergence in response to different wheat diseases.

---

## Introduction

Common wheat (Triticum aestivum L., 2n=6×=42, AABBDD) is a major cereal crop that is consumed by approximately 30% of the global population. Powdery mildew, caused by the obligate biotrophic pathogen Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici (Bgt), poses a significant threat to wheat production, causing yield losses often ranging from 10% to 15% globally1. Dynamic coevolution between pathogens and their hosts frequently renders resistance genes (R genes) ineffective because of the emergence of virulent isolates2. Consequently, dissecting the genetic and molecular mechanisms underlying diversified resistance is essential for disease management.

To date, more than 140 officially named powdery mildew resistance (Pm) genes/alleles (Pm1-Pm71) have been identified in wheat and its relatives3,4. Among these genes, the majority encode typical nucleotide-binding domain leucine-rich repeat (NLR) proteins, which play a central role in plant immunity by recognizing pathogen-derived effectors and triggering robust defense responses5. These NLR proteins, characterized by a modular architecture comprising an N-terminal signaling domain, a nucleotide-binding (NB) domain, and a leucine-rich repeat (LRR) domain, exhibit remarkable adaptability and specificity. Recent analyses of wheat genomes have revealed the extensive diversity of NLRs, suggesting the existence of up to 7780 unique NLR-encoding genes across the wheat gene pool, although fewer than 10% of these genes have been characterized to date5. In addition to NLRs, a growing number of resistance genes with unique domain architectures have also been identified. These include Pm13, encoding a kinase fusion protein6,7; Pm4, encoding a chimeric protein with serine-threonine kinase and C2 domains8; Pm24, Pm36, Pm57, and WTK4, encoding tandem kinase proteins9–12; Pm38/Yr18/Lr34/Sr57, encoding ATP-binding cassette transporter13; and Pm46/Yr46/Lr67/Sr55, encoding a hexose transporter14. Currently, NLR genes remain the primary focus of resistance breeding because of their dominant role in conferring race-specific immunity through direct or indirect effector recognition and their high potential for enhancing disease resistance in wheat breeding programs.

The cloning of wheat genes has long been hindered by the complex genome and evolutionary history of this allohexaploid species. Challenges such as large fragment deletion, insertion and duplication on chromosomes between different Triticum species complicate the gene identification efforts in wheat. Although the rapid development of high-throughput sequencing technologies has accelerated the cloning of wheat genes, abundant structural variations (SVs) among different genotypes are still major obstacles to gene identification in complex genomes3. To address these challenges, sequencing of the donor genome/transcriptome and de novo assembly have proven effective in mitigating issues arising from genomic variation, thereby expediting the identification of target genes. For instance, sequencing trait-associated mutations (STAM) enabled the cloning of YrNAM, encoding a noncanonical resistance protein with a NAM domain and a ZnF-BED domain15; transcriptome sequencing analysis of the loss-of-function mutants of the donor enabled the cloning of Pm13, encoding a mixed lineage kinase domain-like (MLKL) protein from Aegilops longissima in a wheat background. PacBio SMRT long-read genome sequencing allowed the cloning of Pm36, which was generated from a ~900 kb insertion and absent in available wheat reference genomes; and similar uses of this strategy also facilitated the cloning of Pm6916 and Yr2717, demonstrating the power of advanced sequencing techniques in overcoming the inherent challenges of wheat gene cloning.

T. timopheevii (Zhuk.) Zhuk. subsp. timopheevii and its wild form T. timopheevii subsp. armeniacum (Jakubz.) van Slageran (AtAtGG, 2n=28) are the close species of common wheat and possesses abundant disease resistance genes, such as the stem rust (Sr) resistance genes Sr36 and Sr3718; the leaf rust (Lr) resistance genes Lr1819 and Lr5020; and the Pm genes Pm621, Pm2722, and Pm3723. Among them, Pm37 was originally reported to be derived from T. timopheevii and was subsequently transferred into the common wheat background to develop the hexaploid germplasm line NC99BGTAG1123. NC99BGTAG11 is resistant to powdery mildew, making Pm37 a valuable genetic resource for wheat improvement23. Pm37 was preliminarily mapped to a 1.0 cM genetic interval on the chromosome arm 7AL23.

In this work, we clone Pm37 from NC99BGTAG11 by employing an integrated strategy combining map-based cloning and De novo genome sequencing. Pm37 resistance is mediated by a typical CC-NBS-LRR receptor. Pm37 plays a critical role in triggering cell death, mainly mediated by its CC domain. Pm37 may be originally evolved from T. monococcum, and transferred into common wheat through the bridge T. timopheevii. Pm37 is identified as a susceptible allele of the stem rust resistance locus Sr22, and also confers moderate resistance to leaf rust. Collectively, our results uncover a resistance locus whose function diverges through allelic variation, enabling distinct responses to different wheat pathogens.

---

## Results

Map-based cloning of Pm37
For the fine mapping of Pm37, NC99BGTAG11 was crossed with the susceptible wheat parent Wuhuatou to generate a segregating population. Phenotyping of the segregating population across multiple generations using the Bgt isolate E09 revealed a clear monogenic segregation ratio, indicating the suitability of this population for fine mapping (Supplementary Data 1). Two flanking markers, Pm37-G2 and Pm37-163, were first confirmed and used for screening the derivative population comprising 2558 F families of NC99BGTAG11 × Wuhuatou (Supplementary Data 2). We obtained 28 recombinants, which can be used for fine mapping (Supplementary Data 3). Using bulked segregated RNA sequencing (BSR-Seq), more polymorphic markers linked to Pm37 were developed to narrow the fine mapping interval (Supplementary Data 2). Finally, Pm37 was delimited to a 0.0045 cM genetic interval flanked by the markers Pm37-151 and KASP-SNP1 on chromosome arm 7AL, corresponding to a 147.6 kb physical interval referred to the Chinese Spring (CS) reference genome (RefSeq 2.1) (Fig. 1a–c, Supplementary Data 3). Three high-confidence genes were annotated in this interval, including TraesCS7A03G1212600 (encoding a putative B3 domain-containing protein), TraesCS7A03G1212700 (encoding a CC-NBS-LRR, abbreviated as NLR-1), and TraesCS7A03G1212800 (encoding a DYW family of nucleic acid deaminases) (Fig. 1d). We then performed a time-course qRT-PCR analysis of these three genes following inoculation with the Bgt isolate E09. All three genes were expressed in the leaves of both NC99BGTAG11 and Wuhuatou seedlings (Supplementary Fig. 1). Among the three candidates, only TraesCS7A03G1212700 (NLR-1) exhibited higher expression levels in the resistant parent NC99BGTAG11 than in the susceptible parent Wuhuatou across multiple post-inoculation time points, whereas the expression of TraesCS7A03G1212600 and TraesCS7A03G1212800 did not significantly differ between these two genotypes. Homologous sequences of these three genes were then isolated from the cDNA of NC99BGTAG11 and Wuhuatou. No sequence variations were detected in TraesCS7A03G1212600 and TraesCS7A03G1212800 between NC99BGTAG11 and Wuhuatou, suggesting that they were not the Pm37 gene. However, we failed to obtain the full-length sequence of NLR-1 in NC99BGTAG11 after many attempts using a homology-based cloning strategy, indicating possibly complex structural or sequence variations in this interval.

De novo genome assembly of NC99BGTAG11 and candidate gene isolation
To address the above issue, we sequenced NC99BGTAG11 using the PacBio SMRT long-read sequencing approach. PacBio CCS (HiFi) reads corresponding to approximately 16-fold coverage of the CS reference genome were generated. After sequence assembly, 3820 contigs were obtained, with a contig N50 of 25.7 Mb and N90 of 5.3 Mb. The longest contig length was 202.2 Mb, and the total length of the genome assembly was 14.6 Gb, covering the whole genome of the CS reference genome. Those assembly contigs were further scaffolded to chromosome level using RagTag with the CS reference genome, achieving a 98.5% scaffolding rate (Supplementary Data 4). A 17.9 Mb contig spanning the entire Pm37 physical mapping interval was captured by aligning the flanking markers Pm37-151 and KASP-SNP1 around the Pm37 locus (Fig. 1e). Comparison of the target interval among the Triticeae genomes of T. monococcum TA299 and common wheat CS indicated that no new gene was present (Fig. 1d).

Combining the information from PacBio SMRT long-read sequencing, we obtained the full-length sequence of NLR-1 in NC99BGTAG11. Sequence alignment revealed 287 SNPs and 88 InDels between NC99BGTAG11 and Wuhuatou (Supplementary Data 5). A structural variation was identified in the second intron of NLR-1: compared to the susceptible allele in IWGSC RefSeq v2.1, an approximately 3000 bp fragment insertion was present in NC99BGTAG11, which was then validated by PCR amplification and Sanger sequencing (Supplementary Fig. 2). Therefore, NLR-1 was considered as the pivotal candidate gene for Pm37. The full-length sequence of NLR-1 is 9012 bp from the start codon to the stop codon and contains a coding sequence (CDS) of 2808 bp with four exons (Supplementary Fig. 2a).

Validation of NLR-1 by loss-of-function mutants
To clarify whether NLR-1 is required for the resistance to powdery mildew, we screened 894 M2 lines derived from ethyl methanesulfonate (EMS) mutagenesis of NC99BGTAG11 using the Bgt isolate E09, and obtained five independent susceptible homozygous mutant lines (Fig. 2a). All five independent susceptible mutants had SNPs in NLR-1 that resulted in amino acid substitutions or premature stop codons (Fig. 2b). Among them, Mut-1 was a nonsense mutation that produced premature stop codons at the 616th amino acid, resulting in the loss of the entire LRR domain; a SNP was detected in the CC domain of Mut-3, causing p.E46K; Mut-2 and Mut-4 harbored missense mutations with c.C1120T and c.G626A, leading to p.P374S and p.G209D in the NB-ARC domain, respectively; and Mut-5 had a missense point mutation producing p.G494D and a synonymous point mutation of c.G2070A. Structural analysis demonstrated that variations of NLR-1 in these five mutant lines all resulted in three-dimensional (3D) structural changes in the encoded protein (Fig. 2c).

Silencing of NLR-1 eliminates the powdery mildew resistance of NC99BGTAG11
To further validate whether NLR-1 mediates resistance to powdery mildew, we used barley stripe mosaic virus-induced gene silencing (BSMV-VIGS) to specifically knock down the expression of NLR-1 in NC99BGTAG11. qRT-PCR analysis revealed that the expression level of NLR-1 was reduced by 77%–92% in the silenced plants treated with BSMV:NLR-1, revealing the high efficiency of the BSMV-VIGS system (Fig. 2d). After inoculation with the Bgt isolate E09, obvious fungal sporulation occurred on the leaves of the silenced plants, whereas no spores were observed on the leaves of the plants treated with the empty vector BSMV:00 (Fig. 2e, f). These results indicated that the silencing of NLR-1 compromised the powdery mildew resistance of NC99BGTAG11.

Stable transformation of NLR-1 results in a high level of powdery mildew resistance
To further validate whether NLR-1 is sufficient to confer powdery mildew resistance, we transformed a susceptible wheat cultivar Fielder with the CDS of NLR-1 driven by the maize ubiquitin (Ubi) promoter using Agrobacterium-mediated transformation (Fig. 3a). A total of 10 independent positive T0 transgenic plants were identified by PCR and qRT-PCR analysis (Supplementary Fig. 3) and subsequently self-pollinated to produce the T1 generation. Similar to NC99BGTAG11, these positive T1 progenies were immune to the Bgt isolate E09 and an additional 30 tested Bgt isolates (Fig. 3b and Supplementary Data 6). These results demonstrate that NLR-1 is sufficient to confer powdery mildew resistance and serves as the functional allele underlying Pm37.

Expression profile of Pm37
From 2014–2024, NC99BGTAG11 was tested against a total of 108 Bgt isolates collected from different years and regions in China. NC99BGTAG11 displayed immune activity to all the Bgt isolates with infection type (IT) 0 at the seedling stage (Supplementary Data 7). Moreover, NC99BGTAG11 was also immune to 30 mixed Bgt isolates at the adult plant stage under the field conditions in different regions of China over the past decade.

We also traced the pathological index after inoculation with the Bgt isolate E09. No visible spores were detected on the leaves of NC99BGTAG11 at any time, whereas Wuhuatou was highly susceptible, with abundant visible spores and secondary hyphae in the time course of 0–72 h post-inoculation (hpi) (Fig. 4a), in parallel with the increased concentration of H2O2 in NC99BGTAG11 (Fig. 4b). These results suggest the involvement of Pm37 in the regulation of cell death and pathogen defense responses. To further characterize the expression profile of Pm37, we performed qRT-PCR analysis across different tissues. The results revealed that the expression of Pm37 was greatest in the flag leaves, which can further protect the leaves from Bgt destruction for grain-filling (Fig. 4c). Moreover, the expression of Pm37 in NC99BGTAG11 was upregulated by Bgt infection, peaked at 8 hpi, and then maintained a higher expression level than that in Wuhuatou (Fig. 4d), which was relatively low and stable throughout the whole experiment.

We subsequently evaluated the impact of Pm37 on the expression of seven main pathogenesis-related (PR) genes (PR1, PR2, PR3, PR4, PR5, PR9, and PR10) involved in plant defense in NC99BGTAG11 and Wuhuatou at different times after inoculation with the Bgt isolate E09. Significant up-regulation of these PR genes was observed in NC99BGTAG11 upon Bgt invasion, peaking at later time-points than Pm37, except for PR4, whose expression peaked at 6 hpi (Fig. 4e). The coordinated expression patterns of Pm37 and these PR genes demonstrated the active role of Pm37 in plant immunity against fungal infection and suggested that Pm37 can trigger the pathway of the powdery mildew defense response soon after Bgt invasion.

PM37 mediates cell death-inducing activity analysis
PM37 and its individual functional domains (CC, NBS, LRR) and domain combinations (CC-NBS, NBS-LRR) were transiently overexpressed in Nicotiana benthamiana via Agrobacterium-mediated infiltration. The results demonstrated that overexpression of full-length PM37 induced obvious cell death in N. benthamiana leaves. Both the CC domain alone and the CC-NBS domain combination of PM37 were also capable of triggering cell death in N. benthamiana. In contrast, overexpression of the single NBS domain, single LRR domain, or NBS-LRR domain combination failed to induce any observable cell death in N. benthamiana leaves. These results indicate that the cell death-inducing activity of PM37 in N. benthamiana is mainly mediated by its CC domain (Supplementary Fig. 4).

Functional divergence of Pm37
Phylogenetic analysis revealed that Pm37 was an allele of Sr22 locus, which was derived from T. monococcum (Fig. 5a). PM37 and SR22b shared 94.22% of amino acid sequence identity, but distinct functional divergence occurred (Supplementary Data 8). Specifically, Pm37 confers resistance to powdery mildew but susceptibility to stem rust (Fig. 5b), while Sr22 locus was resistant to stem rust but susceptible to powdery mildew (Fig. 5c). Sequence alignment also revealed that PM37 shared the diagnostic amino acids for the stem rust-susceptible alleles (V384L, S608F/Y and G658D), which was consistent with its stem rust-susceptible phenotype (Supplementary Data 8). Further multiple disease assessment revealed that NC99BGTAG11 and NLR-1 transgenic lines were susceptible to all the 14 tested Puccinia striiformis f. sp. tritici (Pst) races, which cause stripe rust (Supplementary Data 9). However, when tested with seven Puccinia triticina (Pt) races that cause leaf rust, NC99BGTAG11 and NLR-1 transgenic lines conferred specifically moderate resistance to the Pt race THDS, while the transgenic receptor Fielder was susceptible (Fig. 5d). In conclusion, NLR-1 produces rare allelic variation-driven functional divergence in response to different wheat pathogens.

Allelic variations of Pm37 in diverse germplasms
To evaluate the allelic variations of Pm37 in diverse germplasms, the homologous sequence of NLR-1 was amplified from 144 wheat accessions and wheat relative accessions, including 36 einkorn wheat, 42 emmer wheat, seven T. timopheevii accessions and 59 hexaploid wheat accessions. Target bands were produced in only five einkorn wheat, three emmer wheat, one T. timopheevii and 15 hexaploid wheat (Supplementary Data 10). Sequence alignment revealed complex sequence variations in this gene among these accessions, including 104 SNPs and nine InDels. These variations are distributed across all the functional domains (CC, NB-ARC, and LRR) of PM37 protein, with effects such as premature stop codons, amino acid substitutions in key functional regions, and frame shifts. Furthermore, these 24 accessions are classified into five haplotypes according to their major sequence variations (Supplementary Data 10). Consistent sequence variations were identified between NC99BGTAG11 and susceptible types, including a 6 bp deletion at the 270-275 position, G284A, G1104A and C2392G. Presumably, these variations are pivotal for the resistance of Pm37, and could be used as diagnostic sequences for the powdery mildew-resistant alleles. Using this information, we further observed that Sr22b possesses susceptibility alleles at these loci, which is consistent with its susceptibility to powdery mildew. Moreover, identical genomic sequences and CDS of NLR-1 as HapI were detected in one T. monococcum accession AA359 (CWI18758), and one T. timopheevii (Zhuk.) Zhuk. subsp. timopheevii accession AAGG477 (CWI17281) (Supplementary Data 10). Powdery mildew phenotype assessment also indicated that AA359 and AAGG477 were both immune to all the 31 tested Bgt isolates as same as Pm37 donor NC99BGTAG11 and the transgenic lines (Supplementary Data 11).

Evolutionary tracing of Pm37
To explore the possible donor of Pm37, the chromosome 7A sequence of NC99BGTAG11 was aligned to the genomes of T. monococcum (accession TA299) and T. timopheevii (accession PI 94760). Five genomic segments (in total 14.2 Mb) of NC99BGTAG11 on the terminal of chromosome arm 7AL were identified exhibiting high similarity to the corresponding region of TA299. Furthermore, we found that Pm37 was derived from a 2.2 Mb introgressed segment from the chromosome 7A of T. monococcum (Fig. 1e). In contrast, no alignment (≥150 kb) was identified between NC99BGTAG11 and T. timopheevii PI 94760 on chromosome 7A (Fig. 6a–c). Although no NLR-1 sequence was identified in T. timopheevii accession PI 94760, NLR-1 was isolated from another T. timopheevii accession AAGG477 (Supplementary Data 10). Taken together, we speculated that Pm37 in the hexaploid line NC99BGTAG11 may be originally derived from T. monococcum and then transferred into bread wheat through T. timopheevii. Additionally, homologs or alleles alignment of Pm37 in different A subgenomes revealed Pm37 clusters with Tm.TA299.r1.7AG0168310 from T. monococcum TA299 (Fig. 6d), further confirming the T. monococcum origin.

Development of diagnostic marker and elite introgression lines for Pm37
To facilitate the detection of Pm37 on the basis of its unique variations, a diagnostic InDel marker, Pm37-FM, was developed based on the unique sequence polymorphism in the second intron. Amplification with this PCR marker generated an amplicon of 473 bp only when the gene Pm37 was present (Supplementary Fig. 5). Using this diagnostic marker, we developed a series of advanced breeding lines carrying Pm37 in different genetic backgrounds, such as the cultivars Shixin 828, Kenong 199, Yannong 999 and Yannong 199. Field investigation of these advanced breeding lines revealed no obvious negative effects on key agronomic or yield traits, such as spike length, spike numbers per plant, spikelet numbers per spike, kernel numbers per spike or thousand-kernel weight (Supplementary Data 12).

---

## Methods

Plant materials
The wheat line NC99BGTAG11 (Reg. no. GP-729, PI 615588), which is available in the United States Department of Agriculture Agricultural Research Service, is an F7-derived line with the pedigree “Saluda”*3/PI 427315, of which Saluda is a soft red winter wheat, and PI 427315 is a T. timopheevii accession34. It carries a single dominant gene, Pm37, that confers resistance to powdery mildew and has been mapped to a 1.0 cM genetic interval on chromosome arm 7AL23. The F1, F2, and F2:3 segregating populations were developed from a cross between NC99BGTAG11 and the Chinese landrace Wuhuatou, which is susceptible to all Bgt isolates tested in our laboratory. The spring wheat cultivar Fielder, which is susceptible to powdery mildew, was used as the transgenic receptor. The wheat accession Sr22TB (donor of Sr22a) and three transgenic families T3-Tm514-2, T3-Tm515-6, and T3-Tm517-1 homozygous for the Sr22b transgene, provided by Prof. Shisheng Chen from the Peking University Institute of Advanced Agricultural Sciences35, were used as a positive control for stem rust resistance evaluation and for analyzing the functional divergence between Pm37 and Sr22, respectively. Wheat samples for haplotype analysis, including five einkorn wheat, three emmer wheat, one T. timopheevii accession and 15 hexaploid wheat accessions, were provided by Prof. Hongxing Xu, Henan University, Kaifeng, China (Supplementary Data 10). The common wheat cultivar Tainong 18 was used as the susceptible control and spreader of Bgt isolates in the phenotype assessment against powdery mildew.

Phenotyping of powdery mildew response
A total of 108 Bgt isolates from different wheat-producing regions in China were used to evaluate the wheat accessions for resistance against powdery mildew (Supplementary Data 7). Among these Bgt isolates, the Bgt isolate E09 was used for phenotyping of NC99BGTAG11, Wuhuatou and their genetic segregating populations, EMS-induced mutants of NC99BGTAG11, and Pm37 transgenic and BSMV-VIGS plants. To map Pm37, more than 20 seedlings of each F2:3 family were used for phenotype evaluation using Bgt isolate E09. At least 20 individuals of the T1 transgenic lines were inoculated with Bgt isolate E09, and another 30 Bgt isolates (Supplementary Data 6). For the evaluations, wheat seedlings at the two-leaf stage were inoculated with Bgt isolates by dusting fungal conidiospores from Tainong 18 leaves36,37. Disease severity was evaluated 14 days after inoculation on a scale from IT 0 to IT 4, where ITs 0, 0;, 1, and 2 indicated a resistant phenotype, and ITs 3 and 4 corresponded to a susceptible reaction38.

Fine mapping of Pm37
To fine map Pm37, equal amounts of RNA from 30 homozygous resistant and 30 homozygous susceptible F2:3 plants of the cross NC99BGTAG11 × Wuhuatou, were mixed to construct the resistant and susceptible bulks, respectively. cDNA libraries of NC99BGTAG11, Wuhuatou, and the two bulks were constructed using TruSeq Stranded mRNA LT Sample Prep Kits (Illumina, San Diego, CA, USA). High-quality cDNA libraries were subsequently sequenced using an Illumina HiSeq 4000 at Beijing Biomarker Technologies Co., Ltd. (Beijing, China). A minimum of 30 Gb of clean data for each bulk and 10 Gb for each parent was set as the thresholds for data production. Afterwards, the sequence alignment, SNP calling, calculation of the ΔSNP index for each SNP, conformation of the candidate intervals and development of polymorphic markers and genotyping detection were performed39. The linkage relationship between polymorphic markers and Pm37 was established using Mapmaker 3.0 software, with the Kosambi map function and the logarithm of odd (LOD) score threshold was set at 3.040. Putative genes were identified through preexisting annotations retrieved through JBrowse (http://202.194.139.32/jbrowse.html) and Ensembl Plants (http://plants.ensembl.org).

PacBio HiFi sequencing and genome assembly of the Pm37 donor
Fresh leaf tissues of NC99BGTAG11 were sampled at the four-leaf stage for DNA extraction and purity assessment following an established procedure11. Eligible DNA with an appropriate size range (15–20 kb) was used for the construction of PacBio HiFi sequencing libraries and subsequent sequencing on the Pacific Biosciences Revio system using HiFi sequencing protocols at Novogene Bioinformatics Technology Co., Ltd (Beijing, China). Libraries were sequenced on three PacBio SMART cells, and more than 90 Gb of data was produced in each cell. A primary assembly was generated from those HiFi sequencing reads using hifiasm (v0.20.0)41. Using RagTag (v2.1.0)42 and the T. aestivum (CS) reference (RefSeq 2.1)43, the assembly contigs were scaffolded to the chromosome level.

Genome-wide alignment analysis with T. monococcum and T. timopheevii
The RagTag-scaffold of chromosome 7A of NC99BGTAG11 was aligned to the reference genomes of T. monococcum TA29944, and T. timopheevii PI 9476045 using MUMmer (v4.0.0rc1)46. The resulting alignments were stringently filtered (≥10 kb, ≥90% identity) to ensure high accuracy of introgression identification. To define contiguous introgressed segments, a more stringent 150 kb length filter was applied, and adjacent retained alignments were merged into blocks with a maximum gap of 200 kb.

Extraction of RNA and qRT-PCR
To investigate the expression patterns of the candidate genes of Pm37 and the pathogenesis-related genes PR1, PR2, PR3, PR4, PR5, PR9 and PR1047, total RNA was extracted from two-leaf-stage leaves of NC99BGTAG11 and Wuhuatou inoculated with the Bgt isolate E09 at 0, 0.5, 2, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 24, 36, 48, and 72 hpi using a FastPure Universal Plant Total RNA Isolation Kit (TransGen, Beijing, China) following the instructions. Furthermore, to determine the expression pattern of the Pm37 gene in different tissues, total RNA was extracted from flag leaves, second leaves from the top, third leaves from the top, fourth leaves from the top, fifth leaves from the top, spikes, stems, and sheaths. Approximately 2 μg of RNA was used for reverse transcription to produce cDNA with a HiScript® III 1st Strand cDNA Synthesis Kit (+gDNA wiper) (Vazyme, Nanjing, China). The qRT-PCR assays were performed using ChamQ Universal SYBR qPCR Master Mix (Vazyme, Nanjing, China) on a Bio-Rad CFX Connect real-time PCR system (Bio-Rad, USA). The relative expression level per gene was calculated as the fold change using the comparative CT method48. Three technical replications of each sample were performed. The gene TaActin was used as the internal control for standardization. Statistically significant differences: two-way ANOVA with Tukey’s test, ns, not significant; *, P<0.05; **, P<0.01; ***, P<0.001; ****, P<0.0001. Primers used in this study are listed in Supplementary Data 2.

EMS mutagenesis and mutant validation
To produce loss-of-function mutants, 4672 seeds of NC99BGTAG11 were first soaked in distilled water for 18 hours at room temperature. Afterwards, they were immersed in freshly prepared 0.8% EMS on a shaker for 14 hours. Prior to sowing, the treated seeds were rinsed with running water for 12 h and dried in a fume hood49. These treated seeds were then sown in the field to produce M2 plants, and a total of 894 M2 plants were harvested. To screen for loss-of-function mutants, the response of each M3 family to the Bgt isolate E09 was tested. The susceptible plants were transplanted into the field to harvest the M4 generation, which was used for phenotypic verification using the same Bgt isolate. To verify the candidate genes, the homologous genomic sequences of candidate gene(s) in these mutants were amplified and then compared for nucleotide variations with those of NC99BGTAG11 by multiple sequence alignment using DNAMAN 8 software (Lynnon Biosoft, San Ramon, CA, USA). Furthermore, the amino acid sequences of Pm37 in NC99BGTAG11 and its mutants were used as inputs to predict the 3D structure of Pm37, and AlphaFold v3.0 was used to model the 3D structure of PM3750. A 3D structure diagram was generated using PyMOL (v.2.6.0) to visualize the molecular structure.

BSMV-VIGS
To silence the candidate gene of Pm37, a 245-bp specific sequence within its CC domain was identified through sequence alignment and selected as the target for silencing (Supplementary Data 13). This fragment was then amplified and inserted in reverse orientation into the barley stripe mosaic virus RNA to generate the recombinant vector BSMV:Pm37. Infected NC99BGTAG11 harboring the empty vector BSMV:00 was used as the negative control47. When the plants grew to the two-leaf stage, the second leaves of the plants were inoculated with the barley stripe mosaic virus9. At 7–12 days post inoculation (dpi), the plants were inoculated with the Bgt isolate E09. Approximately 14 days later, the powdery mildew reactions were evaluated with the 0-4 standard as described above. Spore development was observed with Coomassie blue staining. Relative expression levels of Pm37 in the lines NC99BGTAG11 treated with BSMV:00 (control) and BSMV:Pm37 were examined by qRT-PCR. The expression values are presented as the means ± SDs of three biological replicates and three technical replicates for each leaf. Statistically significant differences: two-way ANOVA with Tukey’s test, ns, not significant; *, P<0.05; **, P<0.01; ***, P<0.001; ****, P<0.0001.

Stable transformation of the candidate gene
The CDS of the candidate gene flanked by a BamHI restriction site was amplified via PCR from the ZTOPO-Blunt/TA-Pm37_CDS construct and cloned into the BamHI site of the pWMB110 vector downstream of the maize (Zea mays L.) ubiquitin (Ubi) promoter with the nopaline synthase (Nor) terminator via the ClonExpress II One Step Cloning Kit (Vazyme, Nanjing, China) to generate the overexpression vector ProUbi:Pm37. The colonies were subsequently sequenced to confirm the accuracy of the cDNA insertions. The ProUbi:Pm37 plasmid was subsequently transformed into the Agrobacterium tumefaciens strain EHA105, which was subsequently transformed into the susceptible wheat cultivar Fielder51. The transgenic plants were confirmed by PCR amplification and gene sequencing. T0 plants and more than 10 plants of each T1 transgenic family were first tested for their responses to the Bgt isolate E09, and then the resistant T1 plants were further assessed using an additional 30 Bgt isolates, with NC99BGTAG11 and Fielder used as controls. The expression patterns of the transgenic plants were also measured using qRT-PCR. Leaves of each T0 seedling plant at the two-leaf stage were collected. TaActin was used as an endogenous control. All the primers used for vector construction, confirmation of positive transgenic plants, and gene expression are listed in Supplementary Data 2.

Cell death assay in N. benthamiana
Pm37 and its domains were constructed into the pS1300-NOS vector for overexpression in N. benthamiana, respectively. Agrobacterium-mediated transient expression was conducted following the method described by Liu et al. with slight modifications52. In brief, Agrobacterium tumefaciens GV3101 strains carrying the specified vector constructs were cultured at 28 °C in Luria-Bertani medium (containing 0.5% yeast extract, 0.25% NaCl, 1% tryptone) with Kanamycin sulfate and rifampicin. The cultures were then centrifuged, and the pellets were resuspended in infiltration buffer (composed of 10 mM MgCl2, and 10 mM MES [pH 5.7]), supplemented with 200 μM acetosyringone. The suspensions were adjusted to an OD600 of 0.8 using the same infiltration buffer and incubated at room temperature for 2–3 h prior to infiltration. Leaves of approximately 4-week-old N. benthamiana plants were infiltrated, with each strain infiltrated into three leaves from different plants. After infiltration, plants were kept under controlled conditions in growth chambers and photographed at 48 hpi53.

Sequence and haplotype analysis
Wheat and its relatives54, including five einkorn wheat accessions, three emmer wheat accessions, one T. timopheevii accession, and 15 hexaploid wheat accessions, were used for haplotype analysis. They were first evaluated by 31 different Bgt isolates to analyze the resistance spectrum as mentioned above (Supplementary Data 11). PacBio HiFi sequencing and genome assembly of the Pm37 donor NC99BGTAG11 provided a high-quality genomic reference. This assembly allowed to accurately identify the CDS of Pm37, enabling the design of highly specific primers targeting conserved regions within the CDS. The PCR primer pairs used for amplifying the entire Pm37 gene are listed in Supplementary Data 2. Total RNA was extracted from each accession, and cDNA was synthesized as the template for amplification. The amplification was performed in a 50 μl reaction mixture containing 25 μl of 2× TransStart FastPfu PCR SuperMix (+dye) (TransGen, Beijing, China), 12 ng of each primer, and 250 ng of genomic DNA. DNA amplification was performed at 95 °C for 3 min, followed by 35 cycles at 95 °C for 15 s, 55–58 °C for 15 s depending on the annealing temperatures of the primer pairs, and 72 °C for 30 s/kb, with a final extension at 72 °C for 5 min. All the PCR products were Sanger sequenced at Sangon Biotech (Shanghai, China) Co., Ltd. The sequences were assembled and aligned using SeqMan Pro in the LaserGene 11 package.

Phylogenetic analysis
The protein sequences encoded by cloned wheat NLR resistance genes, including 30 Pm genes, 12 Sr genes, seven Lr genes, and two Yr genes, were obtained from the NCBI database (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/). These genes were selected based on their confirmed NLR domain architecture to ensure sequence homology. For multiple sequence alignment, we utilized MEGA11 and specifically chose the Align by MUSCLE (Codons) option. After the alignment, poorly aligned regions were manually trimmed to ensure the reliability of subsequent analyses. The phylogenetic cladogram of PM37 with these NLR resistance proteins was constructed using the neighbor-joining method in MEGA11, with the JTT substitution model and 1000 bootstrap replicates to assess branch reliability (node values represent bootstrap support values, indicating the reliability of the topological relationships)55. The cladogram was visualized using iTOL (https://itol.embl.de/)56.

Phenotype divergence assessment for powdery mildew, stem rust, stripe rust and leaf rust
To further determine the relationship between Pm37 and Sr22, the response of the transgenic lines carrying Pm37 and transgenic lines carrying Sr22b to stem rust and powdery mildew was tested using the Chinese Puccinia graminis f. sp. tritici (Pgt) race 34C3RKGQM and the Bgt isolate E09, respectively. Moreover, to explore whether Pm37 is resistant to other diseases, the transgenic lines carrying Pm37 were also inoculated with seven Pt races, including THKS, PHJT, DGJT, PCTT, THTT, THDS and THTS, which cause leaf rust and 14 Pst races, which cause stripe rust (Supplementary Data 9). At least 10 individuals of each transgenic line were inoculated using NC99BGTAG11 and Fielder as controls. Inoculation and phenotype assessment of powdery mildew were performed as described above. Inoculation and phenotype assessment of stem rust were carried out following the procedure previously reported by Luo et al. with minor modifications35: Inoculation was conducted in the greenhouse when the first leaf was fully expanded, after which it was incubated at 25 °C/8 h darkness 22 °C for 16 h. And, 12-14 dpi later, the ITs were recorded on the 0–4 scale57. Inoculation and phenotype assessment of leaf rust were performed in Hebei Agricultural University, Baoding, China, according to previously described methods as Liu et al.58. Inoculation was conducted in the greenhouse when the first leaf was fully expanded. Inoculated seedlings were then incubated at 18–22 °C and 100% relative humidity (RH) for about 24 h. They were then transferred to a growth chamber maintained under 12 h darkness/12 h light at 18–22 °C and 70% RH. Inoculation and phenotype assessment of stripe rust were carried out at the Institute of Plant Protection, Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences, Beijing, China, following the procedure previously reported by Li et al.59. Inoculation was conducted under controlled conditions of 20 °C, 80% humidity and 14 h daily light when the plants were at the fully expanded one-leaf stage, and fresh urediniospores suspended in an aqueous solution containing 0.05% v/v Tween 20 were used for this process. After inoculation, the seedlings were placed in a dew chamber at 10 °C for 24 h and then transferred into a controlled greenhouse with a diurnal cycle of 14 h light at 18 °C and 10 h darkness at 12 °C. ITs were determined on a 0–4 scale57. All the phenotypic assessments were performed at least three independent replications.

Detection of H2O2 reactions and plant cell death
To detect the accumulation of H2O2, the first leaves were collected from NC99BGTAG11 and Wuhuatou at 0, 0.5, 2, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 24, 36, 48, and 72 hpi following invasion of the Bgt isolate E09 and incubated in a 3,3′-diaminobenzidine (DAB) solution (1 mg/mL, pH 5.8) in the dark for 12 h and then bleached in Carnoy’s fixative (absolute alcohol: glacial acetic acid, 3:1, v/v)60. Before the accumulation of H2O2 was assessed, the bleached leaves were incubated in a 0.6% (w/v) Coomassie blue solution for 30 s–120 s and then washed with water. Finally, the samples were observed under an Axioscope 5 microscope (ZEISS, Germany).
To further monitor the invasion process, NC99BGTAG11 and Wuhuatou were inoculated with the Bgt isolate E09, and 2 cm of seedling leaves were collected at 0, 0.5, 2, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 24, 36, 48, and 72 hpi, fixed in 5 mL of Carnoy’s fixative at 37 °C for 24 h, and stained in 5 mL of 0.6% (w/v) Coomassie blue liquid for 5 min. Excess dye on the leaf samples was rinsed with distilled water. Finally, the samples were observed under an Axioscope 5 microscope (ZEISS, Germany).

### Reviewer 2

The manuscript reports isolation of the Pm37 resistance gene from NC99BGTAG11. Authors made good use of standard
genomic tools for fine-mapping to isolate and verify the gene sequence underlying resistance gene, including long read
sequencing of the resistant line NC99BGTAG11. They validate isolation of the Pm37 resistance gene through identification
of EMS mutants, VIGS of Pm37 and stable transgenics. They demonstrate that Pm37 confers resistance to a large collection
of powdery mildew isolates from different parts of China. They also determined that NC99BGTAG11 and Fielder transgenics
having Pm37 are resistant to leaf rust isolates from China. They explore homology of Pm37 derived in this case from
tetraploid T. timopheevii subsp. armeniacum (AtAtGG) with the Sr22 gene that was transferred to common wheat from an A-
genome diploid. They identify two accessions of T. monococcum having an identical Pm37 coding sequence, including
TA299 for which a genome sequence is available. They also identified an accession of T. timopheevii (subsp.
armeniacum?) having Pm37.
Methodology and presentation of cloning results are appropriate. The work is robust and significant in identifying an allele of
Sr22 that confers resistance to powdery mildew and as well as a leaf rust.
The most original and significant aspect of the paper is the determination that Pm37 is an allele of stem rust resistance gene
Sr22 present in both a diploid and tetraploid wheat relative, and that this allele confers resistance to powdery mildew and
leaf rust (but not to stem rust). This result is broadly interesting to wheat researchers as well as those working in other crop
systems. However, there are areas where statements about global utility of Pm37 conferred resistance may be overstated
(see information below).
Overall, the presentation of the manuscript suffers from instances of poor English grammar and language usage. It could be
improved by professional copy editing.
Access to NC99BGTAG11 long read sequence and assembly are necessary to reproduce some results. They do not appear
to be shared.
For all figures having error bars (Figs. 2, 4, S1, and S5), the error bars are not defined in the figure legends.
The presentation of work in Figure S7 is somewhat out of the scope of my expertise. However, the conclusion that
overexpression of the CC domain of Pm37 induced cell death does not seem supported by Figure S7a.
Were Pm37 lines evaluated for resistance to yellow rust? If so, it may be interesting to report a reaction to this rust pathogen
as well.
Figure S2 - The figure legend should include the source of einkron and timopheevii assemblies (TA299 and PI 94760,
respectively) to which NC99BGTAG11 reads were mapped. It is interesting that there were more regions (beyond the
terminal portion of 7AL) where higher read depths were observed between NC99BGTAG11 with wild einkorn TA299 than
with PI 94760. While this may be because PI 94760 is not the donor of Pm37, the overall pattern makes one wonder about
the pedigree of NC99BGTAG11. I would expect more regions of similarity with T. timopheevii in a BC2-derived line. And
fewer with T. monococcum.
Additionally, Fig 1e indicates that the Pm37 region in NC99BGTAG11 is more like TA299 than PI94760. Lines 247 -252
note the Pm37 was derived from T. monococcum via the bridge species T. timopheevii. The authors did find evidence of
Pm37 in the accession of AAGG477 of T. timopheevii (is this an accession of subspecies armeniacum? or subsp
timpopheevii?).
Seed of PI 427315, the T. timopheevii subsp armeniacum parent of the NC99BGTAG11, is available from the USDA
National Small Grains collection. In order to verify that the Pm37 was indeed derived from T. timopheevii, the authors could
include accession PI 427315 in their analysis of allelic variation.
In Figs. 5 and S8, branch lengths appear to be set as equal. Therefore, it would be best to label these as cladograms in the
figure legends. It would be interesting to see these presented as phylograms with bar length indicating sequence similarity.
Rather than comparing with several cloned R genes belonging to other clades in Figure 5, it may be more interesting to
compare Pm37 with the Sr22 alleles/homologs present in A-genome diploids and reported in the Asyraf et al. 2020. At the
least, this paper should be included in the discussion.

Line174-175 - As noted above, the statement about “ultra-broad spectrum powdery mildew resistance at the whole growth

Lines 268- 272 - This sentence suggests that the authors consider T. timopheevii to be in the secondary gene pool of wheat,

It is interesting that recombination rates were quite good in the Pm37 region. This differs somewhat from the Sr22

### Reviewer 4

Review on “Jin et al., Pm37, a susceptible allele of Sr22 from Triticum monocuccm, confers resistance to powdery mildew
and leaf rust in common wheat"
The article from Jin and colleagues describes the cloning of Pm37 in a resistant wheat cultivar (abbreviated NC99 here in
my report) that derives from a cross between a winter wheat and a T. timopheevii accession carrying this gene. The paper
describes the fine mapping steps leading to a very small genetic interval and all the supporting evidence that the candidate
NLR present in the interval is actually the gene controlling the resistance phenotype i.e., production of EMS mutants,
transformation in Fielder, overexpression of the protein with recombined domains. In addition, the paper also describes
sequence analyses performed in order to understand the diversity/evolution of the gene and the locus.
The results about fine mapping and functional validation are interesting, well performed, scientifically sound, and
convincing. In contrast, the sequence analyses and evolutionary interpretations are questionable. Since this later point is my
area of expertise, I will focus my comments/remarks on these aspects which, I think, require significant improvements to be
understood, first, and convincing. I have main concerns about the methods used for sequence analyses and phylogeny.
Please see my remarks below.
## POINT-BY-POINT COMMENTS
I guess there is a generalized mistake with writing the "monococcum" species name here. At several places, the authors
wrote "monocuccm" or even "monocuccum". It requires corrections all along the text and especially in the Title.
# ABSTRACT
- "Pm37 is susceptible to stem rust, and Sr22 is susceptible to powdery mildew".
A gene (or a protein) is not susceptible nor resistant to a disease. A plant is. The writing needs some serious edits.
- "Pm37 and Sr22 produced functional divergence that only overexpression of the CC domain of PM37 and the full length
SR22 could trigger cell-death activity."
I read the sentence several times but cannot make any sense of it.
# INTRODUCTION
- Line 91: A reference is needed when presenting NC99.
# RESULTS
+ Map-based cloning of Pm37
- "comparison of the target interval [..] indicated that no new gene was present (Fig. 1d)."
This is clearly not supported by what is shown at Fig 1d. I found this panel d requires significant improvement so that the
reader is able to understand the Figure by itself. As far as I get it, there are several nonsyntenic genes in the genomes
compared here, no? I see some genes related with "links" and some without link, so I conclude they are non-conserved. In
addition, it is not obvious to me that the genomic segments compared here are the syntenic/orthologous ones. Since the
segments are not flanked by orthologous/collinear genes in all genomes compared, it raises questions. For instance, gene
03G1214100 (CS) could be just next to 168350 (monococcum) but not represented in the segment represented here. Such
comparative genomics picture is not clear if the segments are not bordered by exact collinear genes. To me, it is not possible
to conclude about gene presence/absence based on the work performed here.
+ De novo genome assembly of NC99BGTAG11 and candidate gene isolation
- "Sequence alignment revealed a mass of SNPs and InDels between NC99BGTAG11 and Wuhuatou (Supplementary
Table 4)."
First, the supplemental figures and tables are not numbered, so it is not easy to follow.
Second, Sup Table 4 is cited to support the fact that the two alleles differ a lot. This is a table with 1 line per SNP… A basic
sequence alignment would probably have been much more informative. And in the text, I suggest to just give the numbers of
variations/length or percent identity, which would be much more informative than "a mass".
- Supplemental Fig 3 is misleading with the scale not respected. It must be corrected. It appears that there is a 6 kb intron,
which is somehow unusual in these Triticeae genomes. In CS, this gene is different because this intron is about 2.8kb. Why
not having shown these variations? Is there a TE inserted which would explain this difference? What about monococcum
and timopheevii? This variation could be highly valuable to help with reconstructing haplotypes and trace the origin of the
gene.
Since this gene is almost 9 kb in NC99 versus 6 kb in CS, it is not surprising that all attempts to get a full-length amplicon
systematically failed. This could be added as a probable explanation.
+ Validation of NLR-1 by loss-of-function mutants
- "we […] obtained five independent homozygous mutant lines".
Guess the authors mean five independent "susceptible" homozygous mutant lines.
- Results are convincing. Five susceptible mutants, all with 1 deleterious mutation, perfectly clear.
+ Silencing of NLR-1 eliminated powdery mildew resistance of NC99BGTAG11
Results are convincing. The description of the work performed is, nevertheless, quite expeditive. NLRs are highly repeated
in terms of copy number and silencing 1 single copy is probably not that trivial. I found we lack some details about this
particular NLR, how many copies share similarity etc. what about homeologous copies? And was it obvious to design
probes that specifically target this copy? I suggest to give some more details about that. Although, the previous part with fine
mapping + 5 independent EMS mutants is already quite convincing that this candidate is the causal gene.
+ Stable transformation of NLR-1 produced high level of powdery mildew resistance
Again, expeditive. It would have been interesting, at least, to describe the status of this NLR-1 in the Fielder genome since
an assembled sequence is available.
+ Functional divergence of Pm37
- "PM37 and SR22 shared 94.22% amino acid sequences identity, but occurred distinctly functional divergence
(Supplementary Fig. 6)."
94% aa identity is very low, even lower than what is usually observed between A-B-D homeologs, for instance i.e., genes
that have diverged millions of years ago. Such high level of divergence between genes that are supposed to derive from a
AA common ancestor is questionable. One should not simply conclude that Pm37 is an allele of Sr22. This must be
discussed in regards to "allelic" variations of orthologous genes of AA genomes. This is very unusual and would require
additional analyses before proposing conclusions on the evolution of this gene.
+ Allelic variations of Pm37 in diversified germplasms
The amplification of this gene failed (as explained earlier) in NC99, so why is this limit not considered when trying to amplify
it in 144 accessions? This is a major limit obviously which prevents from concluding on the presence/absence. The Methods
related to that experiment are not detailed enough and it is not possible to evaluate. Maybe the amplification was limited to a
part of the gene only?
- Line 227: "Sequence alignment revealed complex sequence variations in this gene among these accessions".
Why complex?
- Line 230: "sequence variations […] including c. GGAACAC276-282- - - - C - -"
Written as it is here, it is not easy to understand the variation. To me, this is doubtful variation with a single C flanked by 2
indels… This typically due to a problem with the alignment: the C must have been aligned with the last C of GGAACAC. The
indel corresponds to GGAACA only. This is typical from a multiple alignment between sequences that are too variable. The
alignment must be corrected before haplotype classification.
- Line 238: "Additionally, sequence variation analysis of NLR-1 in different wheat […] revealed complex sequence variations
[…]"
Again, same conclusion as the sentence before. "Complex" is not a result. What are the results here?
+ Evolutionary tracing of Pm37
Methods and results are quite questionable. Several remarks:
- First, I suggest a make a Figure showing how the authors identified the introgressed segment.
- Then, why having used read mapping method while there is an assembled genome sequence available? chr7A of NC99
could have been scaffolded (with RagTag or whatever) and compared to chr7A of timopheevii and
monococcum.
- Supplemental Fig 2 is somehow useless and does not provide any evidence of the introgression.
- More importantly, I could not understand the results… In summary it is written: NC99 read mapping revealed similarity over
78Mb (monococcum) and 69Mb (timopheevii), so Pm37 derives from a 32Mb introgressed segment??? How did the author
reach this value? In addition, the Figure 1e does not show any 32Mb or 78Mb segment… and it even shows no similarity
with timopheevii at all… Completely confusing. I suggest to redo the analyses and describe the results in a way that readers
can understand.
- Line 250: "Taking all these information together, we speculated that Pm37 […] was originally derived from T. monocuccm
and transferred into bread wheat through the bridge species T. timopheevii"
I do not see the results supporting this conclusion. There are some T. monococcum with and some without Pm37, so it could
have been inherited from a cross with timopheevii, no?
# DISCUSSION
- "Compared to the susceptible allele in IWGSC RefSeqv2.1, an approximately 4000 bp fragment insertion was present on
the second intron of NLR-1 in NC99BGTAG11."
This is a result not mentioned in the Results section. This is exactly what I have commented above.
# METHODS
- "Putative genes were annotated with the JBrowse pipeline (http://202.194.139.32/jbrowse.html)"
JBrowse is a viewer, not a pipeline for annotating genes. Suggest to clarify.
- "All the sequencing reads were assembled following the established procedure (11)"
Reference 11 is not about HiFi sequence assembly. For bioinformatic analyses, I suggest to describe
tools/methods/thresholds used instead of citing papers that have performed the same type of analyses.
- Line 280: "introduced segments"
Guess the authors mean "introgressed" no?
- "a 204-bp fragment of the gene was amplified and inserted"
For reproducibility purposes, I think it is required to provide the sequence used here for silencing.
- "Sequence and haplotype analysis"
In this paragraph, I do not read any information about sequence analysis or haplotype reconstruction. In contrast, the details
of PCR reactions are given. Methods used for sequence analysis are expected for the results to be reproducible.
- "Phylogenetic analysis"
The methods are not provided again. A tree was built based on a multiple alignment I guess, so methodological details are
needed here. The authors just mention that the tree was built using NJ method. However, all branches of the tree (Figure 5)
have the same length… it is likely a UPGMA tree, no? And this is also the case for the tree provided as a Supplemental
Figure. If UPGMA have been used, I suggest to rebuild the tree with NJ. More importantly, bootstrap values are needed to be
able to conclude on the phylogeny observed.
To me, there is a problem because I suspect that the multiple sequence alignment was computed based on sequences that
somehow do not share any similarity i.e., the 30 Pm, 16 Sr, 10 Lr, and 7 Yr proteins downloaded from NCBI are probably too
divergent to be aligned properly. Or, they were selected on purpose because all these proteins are homologous? In that
case, it must be indicated. But even homologs may contain domains that completely differ. Usually, what is aligned is just
domains that really align (or alignment is cleaned from misaligned positions) so that a tree could be calculated on an
alignment that is correct to calculate genetic distances. So, it looks like what has been done is not scientifically sound. For
instance, STB6 is not a NBS-LRR so I doubt this could be aligned properly with the others. Since evolution of this gene is a
main message of the paper, this part requires significant improvement to be convincing.
# FIGURES
- Fig1: Panel e does not provide any added value to the written message. Suggest to delete or combine with panel d but I am
afraid the two scales are too different.
- Fig5: I doubt a multiple sequence alignment could be computed with such divergent sequences. If yes, this multiple
alignment used for building the tree should be provided.
- There is a confusion between gene IDs between Figures. Gene IDs in trees do not correspond to gene IDs in Fig1 (different
versions). This should be fixed.

## Paper

## Abstract

Wheat relatives harbour abundant variations that can be used for genetic improvement against diseases through complex domestication processes. Here, we report the isolation of the powdery mildew resistance gene Pm37 in common wheat through a strategy integrating map-based cloning, PacBio SMRT long-read genome sequencing, mutagenesis, barley stripe mosaic virus-induced gene silencing and stable transformation. Pm37 encodes a coiled-coil nucleotide-binding site leucine-rich repeat (CC-NBS-LRR) receptor. The cell death-inducing activity of PM37 in Nicotiana benthamiana is mainly mediated by its CC domain. De novo genome sequencing and haplotype analysis reveal that Pm37 may be derived from Triticum monococcum, and transferred into common wheat through T. timopheevii. Interestingly, Pm37 is a susceptible allele of the stem rust resistance locus Sr22, and also confers moderate resistance to leaf rust. Our findings identify a gene characterized by allelic variation-driven functional divergence in response to different wheat diseases.

---

## Introduction

Common wheat (Triticum aestivum L., 2n=6×=42, AABBDD) is a major cereal crop that is consumed by approximately 30% of the global population. Powdery mildew, caused by the obligate biotrophic pathogen Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici (Bgt), poses a significant threat to wheat production, causing yield losses often ranging from 10% to 15% globally1. Dynamic coevolution between pathogens and their hosts frequently renders resistance genes (R genes) ineffective because of the emergence of virulent isolates2. Consequently, dissecting the genetic and molecular mechanisms underlying diversified resistance is essential for disease management.

To date, more than 140 officially named powdery mildew resistance (Pm) genes/alleles (Pm1-Pm71) have been identified in wheat and its relatives3,4. Among these genes, the majority encode typical nucleotide-binding domain leucine-rich repeat (NLR) proteins, which play a central role in plant immunity by recognizing pathogen-derived effectors and triggering robust defense responses5. These NLR proteins, characterized by a modular architecture comprising an N-terminal signaling domain, a nucleotide-binding (NB) domain, and a leucine-rich repeat (LRR) domain, exhibit remarkable adaptability and specificity. Recent analyses of wheat genomes have revealed the extensive diversity of NLRs, suggesting the existence of up to 7780 unique NLR-encoding genes across the wheat gene pool, although fewer than 10% of these genes have been characterized to date5. In addition to NLRs, a growing number of resistance genes with unique domain architectures have also been identified. These include Pm13, encoding a kinase fusion protein6,7; Pm4, encoding a chimeric protein with serine-threonine kinase and C2 domains8; Pm24, Pm36, Pm57, and WTK4, encoding tandem kinase proteins9–12; Pm38/Yr18/Lr34/Sr57, encoding ATP-binding cassette transporter13; and Pm46/Yr46/Lr67/Sr55, encoding a hexose transporter14. Currently, NLR genes remain the primary focus of resistance breeding because of their dominant role in conferring race-specific immunity through direct or indirect effector recognition and their high potential for enhancing disease resistance in wheat breeding programs.

The cloning of wheat genes has long been hindered by the complex genome and evolutionary history of this allohexaploid species. Challenges such as large fragment deletion, insertion and duplication on chromosomes between different Triticum species complicate the gene identification efforts in wheat. Although the rapid development of high-throughput sequencing technologies has accelerated the cloning of wheat genes, abundant structural variations (SVs) among different genotypes are still major obstacles to gene identification in complex genomes3. To address these challenges, sequencing of the donor genome/transcriptome and de novo assembly have proven effective in mitigating issues arising from genomic variation, thereby expediting the identification of target genes. For instance, sequencing trait-associated mutations (STAM) enabled the cloning of YrNAM, encoding a noncanonical resistance protein with a NAM domain and a ZnF-BED domain15; transcriptome sequencing analysis of the loss-of-function mutants of the donor enabled the cloning of Pm13, encoding a mixed lineage kinase domain-like (MLKL) protein from Aegilops longissima in a wheat background. PacBio SMRT long-read genome sequencing allowed the cloning of Pm36, which was generated from a ~900 kb insertion and absent in available wheat reference genomes; and similar uses of this strategy also facilitated the cloning of Pm6916 and Yr2717, demonstrating the power of advanced sequencing techniques in overcoming the inherent challenges of wheat gene cloning.

T. timopheevii (Zhuk.) Zhuk. subsp. timopheevii and its wild form T. timopheevii subsp. armeniacum (Jakubz.) van Slageran (AtAtGG, 2n=28) are the close species of common wheat and possesses abundant disease resistance genes, such as the stem rust (Sr) resistance genes Sr36 and Sr3718; the leaf rust (Lr) resistance genes Lr1819 and Lr5020; and the Pm genes Pm621, Pm2722, and Pm3723. Among them, Pm37 was originally reported to be derived from T. timopheevii and was subsequently transferred into the common wheat background to develop the hexaploid germplasm line NC99BGTAG1123. NC99BGTAG11 is resistant to powdery mildew, making Pm37 a valuable genetic resource for wheat improvement23. Pm37 was preliminarily mapped to a 1.0 cM genetic interval on the chromosome arm 7AL23.

In this work, we clone Pm37 from NC99BGTAG11 by employing an integrated strategy combining map-based cloning and De novo genome sequencing. Pm37 resistance is mediated by a typical CC-NBS-LRR receptor. Pm37 plays a critical role in triggering cell death, mainly mediated by its CC domain. Pm37 may be originally evolved from T. monococcum, and transferred into common wheat through the bridge T. timopheevii. Pm37 is identified as a susceptible allele of the stem rust resistance locus Sr22, and also confers moderate resistance to leaf rust. Collectively, our results uncover a resistance locus whose function diverges through allelic variation, enabling distinct responses to different wheat pathogens.

---

## Results

Map-based cloning of Pm37
For the fine mapping of Pm37, NC99BGTAG11 was crossed with the susceptible wheat parent Wuhuatou to generate a segregating population. Phenotyping of the segregating population across multiple generations using the Bgt isolate E09 revealed a clear monogenic segregation ratio, indicating the suitability of this population for fine mapping (Supplementary Data 1). Two flanking markers, Pm37-G2 and Pm37-163, were first confirmed and used for screening the derivative population comprising 2558 F families of NC99BGTAG11 × Wuhuatou (Supplementary Data 2). We obtained 28 recombinants, which can be used for fine mapping (Supplementary Data 3). Using bulked segregated RNA sequencing (BSR-Seq), more polymorphic markers linked to Pm37 were developed to narrow the fine mapping interval (Supplementary Data 2). Finally, Pm37 was delimited to a 0.0045 cM genetic interval flanked by the markers Pm37-151 and KASP-SNP1 on chromosome arm 7AL, corresponding to a 147.6 kb physical interval referred to the Chinese Spring (CS) reference genome (RefSeq 2.1) (Fig. 1a–c, Supplementary Data 3). Three high-confidence genes were annotated in this interval, including TraesCS7A03G1212600 (encoding a putative B3 domain-containing protein), TraesCS7A03G1212700 (encoding a CC-NBS-LRR, abbreviated as NLR-1), and TraesCS7A03G1212800 (encoding a DYW family of nucleic acid deaminases) (Fig. 1d). We then performed a time-course qRT-PCR analysis of these three genes following inoculation with the Bgt isolate E09. All three genes were expressed in the leaves of both NC99BGTAG11 and Wuhuatou seedlings (Supplementary Fig. 1). Among the three candidates, only TraesCS7A03G1212700 (NLR-1) exhibited higher expression levels in the resistant parent NC99BGTAG11 than in the susceptible parent Wuhuatou across multiple post-inoculation time points, whereas the expression of TraesCS7A03G1212600 and TraesCS7A03G1212800 did not significantly differ between these two genotypes. Homologous sequences of these three genes were then isolated from the cDNA of NC99BGTAG11 and Wuhuatou. No sequence variations were detected in TraesCS7A03G1212600 and TraesCS7A03G1212800 between NC99BGTAG11 and Wuhuatou, suggesting that they were not the Pm37 gene. However, we failed to obtain the full-length sequence of NLR-1 in NC99BGTAG11 after many attempts using a homology-based cloning strategy, indicating possibly complex structural or sequence variations in this interval.

De novo genome assembly of NC99BGTAG11 and candidate gene isolation
To address the above issue, we sequenced NC99BGTAG11 using the PacBio SMRT long-read sequencing approach. PacBio CCS (HiFi) reads corresponding to approximately 16-fold coverage of the CS reference genome were generated. After sequence assembly, 3820 contigs were obtained, with a contig N50 of 25.7 Mb and N90 of 5.3 Mb. The longest contig length was 202.2 Mb, and the total length of the genome assembly was 14.6 Gb, covering the whole genome of the CS reference genome. Those assembly contigs were further scaffolded to chromosome level using RagTag with the CS reference genome, achieving a 98.5% scaffolding rate (Supplementary Data 4). A 17.9 Mb contig spanning the entire Pm37 physical mapping interval was captured by aligning the flanking markers Pm37-151 and KASP-SNP1 around the Pm37 locus (Fig. 1e). Comparison of the target interval among the Triticeae genomes of T. monococcum TA299 and common wheat CS indicated that no new gene was present (Fig. 1d).

Combining the information from PacBio SMRT long-read sequencing, we obtained the full-length sequence of NLR-1 in NC99BGTAG11. Sequence alignment revealed 287 SNPs and 88 InDels between NC99BGTAG11 and Wuhuatou (Supplementary Data 5). A structural variation was identified in the second intron of NLR-1: compared to the susceptible allele in IWGSC RefSeq v2.1, an approximately 3000 bp fragment insertion was present in NC99BGTAG11, which was then validated by PCR amplification and Sanger sequencing (Supplementary Fig. 2). Therefore, NLR-1 was considered as the pivotal candidate gene for Pm37. The full-length sequence of NLR-1 is 9012 bp from the start codon to the stop codon and contains a coding sequence (CDS) of 2808 bp with four exons (Supplementary Fig. 2a).

Validation of NLR-1 by loss-of-function mutants
To clarify whether NLR-1 is required for the resistance to powdery mildew, we screened 894 M2 lines derived from ethyl methanesulfonate (EMS) mutagenesis of NC99BGTAG11 using the Bgt isolate E09, and obtained five independent susceptible homozygous mutant lines (Fig. 2a). All five independent susceptible mutants had SNPs in NLR-1 that resulted in amino acid substitutions or premature stop codons (Fig. 2b). Among them, Mut-1 was a nonsense mutation that produced premature stop codons at the 616th amino acid, resulting in the loss of the entire LRR domain; a SNP was detected in the CC domain of Mut-3, causing p.E46K; Mut-2 and Mut-4 harbored missense mutations with c.C1120T and c.G626A, leading to p.P374S and p.G209D in the NB-ARC domain, respectively; and Mut-5 had a missense point mutation producing p.G494D and a synonymous point mutation of c.G2070A. Structural analysis demonstrated that variations of NLR-1 in these five mutant lines all resulted in three-dimensional (3D) structural changes in the encoded protein (Fig. 2c).

Silencing of NLR-1 eliminates the powdery mildew resistance of NC99BGTAG11
To further validate whether NLR-1 mediates resistance to powdery mildew, we used barley stripe mosaic virus-induced gene silencing (BSMV-VIGS) to specifically knock down the expression of NLR-1 in NC99BGTAG11. qRT-PCR analysis revealed that the expression level of NLR-1 was reduced by 77%–92% in the silenced plants treated with BSMV:NLR-1, revealing the high efficiency of the BSMV-VIGS system (Fig. 2d). After inoculation with the Bgt isolate E09, obvious fungal sporulation occurred on the leaves of the silenced plants, whereas no spores were observed on the leaves of the plants treated with the empty vector BSMV:00 (Fig. 2e, f). These results indicated that the silencing of NLR-1 compromised the powdery mildew resistance of NC99BGTAG11.

Stable transformation of NLR-1 results in a high level of powdery mildew resistance
To further validate whether NLR-1 is sufficient to confer powdery mildew resistance, we transformed a susceptible wheat cultivar Fielder with the CDS of NLR-1 driven by the maize ubiquitin (Ubi) promoter using Agrobacterium-mediated transformation (Fig. 3a). A total of 10 independent positive T0 transgenic plants were identified by PCR and qRT-PCR analysis (Supplementary Fig. 3) and subsequently self-pollinated to produce the T1 generation. Similar to NC99BGTAG11, these positive T1 progenies were immune to the Bgt isolate E09 and an additional 30 tested Bgt isolates (Fig. 3b and Supplementary Data 6). These results demonstrate that NLR-1 is sufficient to confer powdery mildew resistance and serves as the functional allele underlying Pm37.

Expression profile of Pm37
From 2014–2024, NC99BGTAG11 was tested against a total of 108 Bgt isolates collected from different years and regions in China. NC99BGTAG11 displayed immune activity to all the Bgt isolates with infection type (IT) 0 at the seedling stage (Supplementary Data 7). Moreover, NC99BGTAG11 was also immune to 30 mixed Bgt isolates at the adult plant stage under the field conditions in different regions of China over the past decade.

We also traced the pathological index after inoculation with the Bgt isolate E09. No visible spores were detected on the leaves of NC99BGTAG11 at any time, whereas Wuhuatou was highly susceptible, with abundant visible spores and secondary hyphae in the time course of 0–72 h post-inoculation (hpi) (Fig. 4a), in parallel with the increased concentration of H2O2 in NC99BGTAG11 (Fig. 4b). These results suggest the involvement of Pm37 in the regulation of cell death and pathogen defense responses. To further characterize the expression profile of Pm37, we performed qRT-PCR analysis across different tissues. The results revealed that the expression of Pm37 was greatest in the flag leaves, which can further protect the leaves from Bgt destruction for grain-filling (Fig. 4c). Moreover, the expression of Pm37 in NC99BGTAG11 was upregulated by Bgt infection, peaked at 8 hpi, and then maintained a higher expression level than that in Wuhuatou (Fig. 4d), which was relatively low and stable throughout the whole experiment.

We subsequently evaluated the impact of Pm37 on the expression of seven main pathogenesis-related (PR) genes (PR1, PR2, PR3, PR4, PR5, PR9, and PR10) involved in plant defense in NC99BGTAG11 and Wuhuatou at different times after inoculation with the Bgt isolate E09. Significant up-regulation of these PR genes was observed in NC99BGTAG11 upon Bgt invasion, peaking at later time-points than Pm37, except for PR4, whose expression peaked at 6 hpi (Fig. 4e). The coordinated expression patterns of Pm37 and these PR genes demonstrated the active role of Pm37 in plant immunity against fungal infection and suggested that Pm37 can trigger the pathway of the powdery mildew defense response soon after Bgt invasion.

PM37 mediates cell death-inducing activity analysis
PM37 and its individual functional domains (CC, NBS, LRR) and domain combinations (CC-NBS, NBS-LRR) were transiently overexpressed in Nicotiana benthamiana via Agrobacterium-mediated infiltration. The results demonstrated that overexpression of full-length PM37 induced obvious cell death in N. benthamiana leaves. Both the CC domain alone and the CC-NBS domain combination of PM37 were also capable of triggering cell death in N. benthamiana. In contrast, overexpression of the single NBS domain, single LRR domain, or NBS-LRR domain combination failed to induce any observable cell death in N. benthamiana leaves. These results indicate that the cell death-inducing activity of PM37 in N. benthamiana is mainly mediated by its CC domain (Supplementary Fig. 4).

Functional divergence of Pm37
Phylogenetic analysis revealed that Pm37 was an allele of Sr22 locus, which was derived from T. monococcum (Fig. 5a). PM37 and SR22b shared 94.22% of amino acid sequence identity, but distinct functional divergence occurred (Supplementary Data 8). Specifically, Pm37 confers resistance to powdery mildew but susceptibility to stem rust (Fig. 5b), while Sr22 locus was resistant to stem rust but susceptible to powdery mildew (Fig. 5c). Sequence alignment also revealed that PM37 shared the diagnostic amino acids for the stem rust-susceptible alleles (V384L, S608F/Y and G658D), which was consistent with its stem rust-susceptible phenotype (Supplementary Data 8). Further multiple disease assessment revealed that NC99BGTAG11 and NLR-1 transgenic lines were susceptible to all the 14 tested Puccinia striiformis f. sp. tritici (Pst) races, which cause stripe rust (Supplementary Data 9). However, when tested with seven Puccinia triticina (Pt) races that cause leaf rust, NC99BGTAG11 and NLR-1 transgenic lines conferred specifically moderate resistance to the Pt race THDS, while the transgenic receptor Fielder was susceptible (Fig. 5d). In conclusion, NLR-1 produces rare allelic variation-driven functional divergence in response to different wheat pathogens.

Allelic variations of Pm37 in diverse germplasms
To evaluate the allelic variations of Pm37 in diverse germplasms, the homologous sequence of NLR-1 was amplified from 144 wheat accessions and wheat relative accessions, including 36 einkorn wheat, 42 emmer wheat, seven T. timopheevii accessions and 59 hexaploid wheat accessions. Target bands were produced in only five einkorn wheat, three emmer wheat, one T. timopheevii and 15 hexaploid wheat (Supplementary Data 10). Sequence alignment revealed complex sequence variations in this gene among these accessions, including 104 SNPs and nine InDels. These variations are distributed across all the functional domains (CC, NB-ARC, and LRR) of PM37 protein, with effects such as premature stop codons, amino acid substitutions in key functional regions, and frame shifts. Furthermore, these 24 accessions are classified into five haplotypes according to their major sequence variations (Supplementary Data 10). Consistent sequence variations were identified between NC99BGTAG11 and susceptible types, including a 6 bp deletion at the 270-275 position, G284A, G1104A and C2392G. Presumably, these variations are pivotal for the resistance of Pm37, and could be used as diagnostic sequences for the powdery mildew-resistant alleles. Using this information, we further observed that Sr22b possesses susceptibility alleles at these loci, which is consistent with its susceptibility to powdery mildew. Moreover, identical genomic sequences and CDS of NLR-1 as HapI were detected in one T. monococcum accession AA359 (CWI18758), and one T. timopheevii (Zhuk.) Zhuk. subsp. timopheevii accession AAGG477 (CWI17281) (Supplementary Data 10). Powdery mildew phenotype assessment also indicated that AA359 and AAGG477 were both immune to all the 31 tested Bgt isolates as same as Pm37 donor NC99BGTAG11 and the transgenic lines (Supplementary Data 11).

Evolutionary tracing of Pm37
To explore the possible donor of Pm37, the chromosome 7A sequence of NC99BGTAG11 was aligned to the genomes of T. monococcum (accession TA299) and T. timopheevii (accession PI 94760). Five genomic segments (in total 14.2 Mb) of NC99BGTAG11 on the terminal of chromosome arm 7AL were identified exhibiting high similarity to the corresponding region of TA299. Furthermore, we found that Pm37 was derived from a 2.2 Mb introgressed segment from the chromosome 7A of T. monococcum (Fig. 1e). In contrast, no alignment (≥150 kb) was identified between NC99BGTAG11 and T. timopheevii PI 94760 on chromosome 7A (Fig. 6a–c). Although no NLR-1 sequence was identified in T. timopheevii accession PI 94760, NLR-1 was isolated from another T. timopheevii accession AAGG477 (Supplementary Data 10). Taken together, we speculated that Pm37 in the hexaploid line NC99BGTAG11 may be originally derived from T. monococcum and then transferred into bread wheat through T. timopheevii. Additionally, homologs or alleles alignment of Pm37 in different A subgenomes revealed Pm37 clusters with Tm.TA299.r1.7AG0168310 from T. monococcum TA299 (Fig. 6d), further confirming the T. monococcum origin.

Development of diagnostic marker and elite introgression lines for Pm37
To facilitate the detection of Pm37 on the basis of its unique variations, a diagnostic InDel marker, Pm37-FM, was developed based on the unique sequence polymorphism in the second intron. Amplification with this PCR marker generated an amplicon of 473 bp only when the gene Pm37 was present (Supplementary Fig. 5). Using this diagnostic marker, we developed a series of advanced breeding lines carrying Pm37 in different genetic backgrounds, such as the cultivars Shixin 828, Kenong 199, Yannong 999 and Yannong 199. Field investigation of these advanced breeding lines revealed no obvious negative effects on key agronomic or yield traits, such as spike length, spike numbers per plant, spikelet numbers per spike, kernel numbers per spike or thousand-kernel weight (Supplementary Data 12).
